reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it demonstrates an ordinary cryptocurrency workflow: swapping BNB for USDT, bridging the token from BSC to Avalanche, and exchanging the bridged token for AVAX. The speaker gives operational instructions for MetaMask, EvoDeFi and Trader Joe, including importing a token by its public contract address, without promising guaranteed returns or requesting private credentials, recovery phrases or account control.

citations.quote: we take $50, then pancake swap, 50 USDT right go to evoDefi and go from BSC chain, Binance Smart Chain to avalanche
you enter the address- I already got that but then the tokens will show up in your wallet

opening.argument: The bridge interface explicitly links a cryptocurrency bonus to completing a transaction: it says, “we send you bonus 0.001 AVAX with every transaction,” while showing a recipient address, a 50.0 USDT amount, and an approval/send control. That is a concrete reward attached to the viewer’s transfer action, not merely neutral education. The description also directs viewers to use a supplied wallet address before depositing into Splash. Taken together, the presentation encourages viewers to send assets through an externally supplied destination in connection with an advertised benefit, fitting a low-barrier reward acquisition pattern.

citations.quote: consider using my Wave Starter Address before depositing into Splash: 0x3Db0049A26728F77e8aCDB197772A8F54A52E1cC

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the process an ordinary swap does not answer the reward-and-action linkage. The bridge screen pairs the bonus language with the recipient field, asset amount, and approval step. The absence of a guaranteed investment return or a request for recovery phrases is beside the point: a viewer can still be induced to authorize a token transfer by the promise of an easy crypto bonus.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The bridge screen does not establish that the bonus was actually delivered, guaranteed, or conditioned on using the creator’s address. It shows a note on an interface, but the supplied material does not document a payout or an outcome. The description says viewers may “consider using” the address, which is optional wording rather than a demand to transfer funds.

citations.quote: consider using my Wave Starter Address before depositing into Splash: 0x3Db0049A26728F77e8aCDB197772A8F54A52E1cC

opening.argument: Several risk signals appear together: the content directs viewers to PancakeSwap, EvoDeFi, Trader Joe, Telegram, and a supplied wallet address, while instructing them to approve access to tokens and send a crypto amount. The description says to swap BNB for USDT, bridge it, and then deposit using the creator’s address; the narration confirms, “we have to give permission first to access our money.” This combination of external crypto links, wallet authorization, a recipient address, and a promised bonus creates a persuasive transfer funnel even though the amount shown is modest. The educational framing does not remove the financial risk created by these steps.

citations.quote: Swap $BNB (or another coin from your Metamask wallet) for $USDT on Pancakeswap
consider using my Wave Starter Address before depositing into Splash: 0x3Db0049A26728F77e8aCDB197772A8F54A52E1cC
we have to give permission first to access our money

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense’s description of the steps as operational does not neutralize the actual risk signals. The viewer is still directed through multiple external crypto services and asked to authorize access before sending tokens. The screen also displays a bonus claim alongside the transfer flow. A scam assessment can rest on this combination of inducement and authorization risk without requiring a promise of guaranteed profit or a request for private credentials.

citations.quote: we have to give permission first to access our money

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These are ordinary features of the demonstrated workflow, not proof of deception. The narration identifies a swap, a bridge, and a later exchange into AVAX, while the supplied material gives no evidence of stolen credentials, hidden fees beyond the displayed bridge charge, or a failed transfer. “Give permission” describes token approval in the interface; it does not show that private credentials or account control were requested.

citations.quote: we pay like 50 cent in fee 25 cent plus 0.5 %
then the tokens will show up in your wallet

opening.argument: Although presented as a tutorial, the material actively steers viewers toward participation. It supplies direct links to the swap, bridge, and trading services, invites viewers to use the presenter’s wallet address before depositing into Splash, promotes a Telegram project channel, and discloses affiliate links that may earn a commission when viewers click or subscribe. The tutorial format therefore functions as promotional routing into a crypto transaction pathway, with a creator-connected address and financial incentive embedded in the instructions. That is more than detached explanation: it encourages viewers to act through the promoted destinations.

Join my New Projects Corner on Telegram: https://t.me/NewProjectCorner
Some of the links on this webpage are affiliate links, meaning, at no additional cost to you, I may earn a commission if you click through and make a purchase and/or subscribe.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The label of tutorial does not settle its function. The description includes a creator-associated address before a deposit, a Telegram destination, and an affiliate disclosure tied to clicks, purchases, or subscriptions. Those are promotional pathways surrounding the operational instructions. The defense’s claim that no private credentials are requested does not address whether viewers are being steered toward a financially consequential crypto action.

citations.quote: consider using my Wave Starter Address before depositing into Splash: 0x3Db0049A26728F77e8aCDB197772A8F54A52E1cC
I may earn a commission if you click through and make a purchase and/or subscribe.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The cited disclosures support transparency, not concealment: the description expressly identifies the affiliate relationship and says the presenter recommends services believed to be used personally. The address language is “consider using,” and the tutorial explains how to swap and bridge rather than promising earnings. Promotion or monetization alone does not show that the viewer receives a deceptive reward or that the transaction is fraudulent.
